items.stem: Larkspur Supply Co. treats short-term, highly liquid investments as cash equivalents. On December 31, 2026, it held four investments. Which one qualifies as a cash equivalent?
options: A U.S. Treasury note purchased on December 1, 2026, that matures on December 1, 2028
A six-month certificate of deposit purchased on August 15, 2026, that matures on February 15, 2027
A 12-month Treasury bill purchased on January 5, 2026, that had 60 days to maturity at year-end
A U.S. Treasury bill purchased on November 15, 2026, that matures on January 31, 2027
items.rule_line: A cash equivalent has an original maturity of three months or less measured from the date the entity acquires it.

why.A: The original maturity is two years. Maturity is measured from the date of purchase, and this note is far outside the three-month window.
why.B: It had six months to run when purchased. Being within three months of maturity at year-end does not matter; the test is applied at acquisition.
why.C: The original maturity was 12 months. Only investments with an original maturity of three months or less at purchase qualify, even if nearly due at the balance sheet date.
why.D: Correct. A short-term, highly liquid investment with an original maturity of three months or less when acquired is a cash equivalent. This bill had about 2.5 months to run when purchased.

items.task_source: 2026 AICPA Blueprint FAR Area II (group names verified; task wording paraphrased)
items.stem: At December 31, 2026, the bank statement of Cobalt Ridge Inc. showed a balance of $45,600. Cobalt Ridge's records showed deposits in transit of $4,200 and outstanding checks of $7,850. The bank had mistakenly charged Cobalt Ridge's account with a $1,000 check written by another customer. What is Cobalt Ridge's correct cash balance at December 31, 2026?
items.rule_line: On the bank side, add deposits in transit and bank errors that understated the balance; subtract outstanding checks.

why.A: Subtracts the deposits in transit. Deposits recorded by the company but not yet credited by the bank are added to the bank balance.
why.B: Subtracts the bank error instead of adding it back. The check belongs to another customer, so correcting it raises the bank-side balance.
why.C: Omits the bank error. The $1,000 wrongly charged by the bank must be added back to the bank side.
why.D: Correct. Bank balance $45,600 + deposits in transit $4,200 - outstanding checks $7,850 + $1,000 bank error corrected = $42,950.

items.task_source: 2026 AICPA Blueprint FAR Area II (group names verified; task wording paraphrased)
items.stem: Before preparing its December 31, 2026 bank reconciliation, Juniper Hollow Ltd. had a book cash balance of $38,420. The reconciliation revealed: a customer's NSF check of $1,150 returned by the bank; a bank service charge of $45; a customer note of $5,000 collected by the bank together with $150 of interest, neither yet recorded; and a check for $960 to a supplier that was recorded in the books as $690. What is the correct cash balance?
items.rule_line: Adjust book cash for bank-initiated items and book errors: subtract NSF checks and fees, add collections and interest.

why.A: Leaves out the $150 of interest collected by the bank. Interest collected on the note also increases book cash.
why.B: Correct. $38,420 - $1,150 NSF - $45 service charge + $5,150 note and interest - $270 recording error ($960 - $690) = $42,105.
why.C: Adds the $270 error. The check was recorded for too little, so book cash is overstated by $270 and must be reduced.
why.D: Adds the NSF check. A returned customer check reduces book cash.

steps: Check recorded at 690 instead of 960: cash overstated by 270; 42,375 - 270 = 42,105

items.stem: Mesa Verde Corp. holds $30,000 of cash that is contractually restricted for the acquisition of equipment next year, in addition to $200,000 of unrestricted cash and cash equivalents. How should the restricted cash be treated in the statement of cash flows?
options: Movements into restricted cash are shown as investing outflows because the funds cannot be used freely
Restricted cash is excluded from the statement and disclosed only in the notes as a noncash item
Only the unrestricted $200,000 is explained, with restricted cash shown as a separate financing activity line
The statement explains the change in total cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash, so transfers among them are not cash flows
items.rule_line: The statement of cash flows explains the change in cash, cash equivalents and restricted cash combined.

why.A: Some entities did this before the current guidance. Now restricted cash is part of the total the statement explains, so transfers are not investing flows.
why.B: Excluding it would leave the ending total out of line with the amounts on the balance sheet that the statement must reconcile to.
why.C: Restricted cash is not a financing activity. It is grouped with cash and cash equivalents in the beginning and ending totals.
why.D: Correct. Restricted cash is combined with cash and cash equivalents when reconciling beginning and ending balances, and a reconciliation to the balance sheet is disclosed.

items.task: Prepare bank reconciliations; classify cash, cash equivalents, restricted cash and overdrafts
items.task_source: 2026 AICPA Blueprint FAR Area II (group names verified; task wording paraphrased)
items.stem: At December 31, 2026, Redwood Analytics Inc. had a checking account of $30,000 at Bank North and a separate checking account at Bank South that was overdrawn by $5,000 because of outstanding checks. The banks are unrelated and the company has no right of setoff between the accounts. How should Redwood report these balances?
options: Cash of $25,000 and no liability
Cash of $30,000 and a $5,000 reduction of accounts payable
Cash of $35,000 and a current liability of $5,000
Cash of $30,000 and a current liability of $5,000
items.rule_line: Overdrafts are offset against positive balances only at the same bank with a right of setoff; otherwise they are liabilities.

why.A: Nets accounts at unrelated banks with no right of setoff, which understates both cash and liabilities.
why.B: An overdraft is not a reduction of trade payables. Offsetting different kinds of liabilities is not appropriate.
why.C: Adds the overdraft to cash. An overdraft never increases cash.
why.D: Correct. An overdraft at one bank cannot be offset against a balance at a different bank absent a right of setoff. The overdraft is a current liability.

items.stem: Alder Point Company maintains an imprest petty cash fund of $500. When the fund was counted, it contained $132 in currency, a receipt for $160 of postage and a receipt for $190 of office supplies. What amount must the company deposit into the fund to restore it?
items.rule_line: Replenishment equals the imprest amount minus cash on hand; any unsupported difference is charged to cash short and over.

why.A: The currency on hand is not the amount needed to restore the fund. The fund needs $500 - $132.
why.B: Uses only the receipts. The unexplained $18 shortage also has to be replenished and charged to cash short and over.
why.C: Correct. $500 - $132 = $368. Receipts support $350 of postage and supplies, and the unsupported $18 is recorded as cash short.
why.D: Restores the entire fund as though it were empty. The fund still holds $132 of currency.

steps: Receipts support 160 + 190 = 350; the difference of 18 is cash short

items.task_source: 2026 AICPA Blueprint FAR Area II (group names verified; task wording paraphrased)
items.stem: Harbor Point Inc. must keep $80,000 on deposit as a legally restricted compensating balance against a five-year term loan. The deposit is not available for current operations. How should the deposit be reported at December 31, 2026?
options: As part of cash and cash equivalents in current assets
As a current asset because bank deposits are liquid
As an offset against the loan so that the loan is reported net
As a separate noncurrent asset, with the arrangement disclosed
items.rule_line: Legally restricted deposits are classified by the term of the related borrowing and reported separately from unrestricted cash.

why.A: Restricted deposits that cannot be withdrawn for current operations are excluded from unrestricted cash and cash equivalents.
why.B: The restriction ties the deposit to a five-year loan, so classification follows the term of the related debt. Current classification would apply only against short-term borrowing.
why.C: Offsetting requires a right of setoff and intent to settle net. A compensating balance requirement does not meet those conditions.
why.D: Correct. A legally restricted deposit held against long-term borrowing is classified as a separate noncurrent asset and disclosed; it is not cash available for current use.

items.stem: On December 31, 2026, Quarry Gate Inc. recorded $6,000 of checks to suppliers as reducing cash and accounts payable, but the checks were not mailed until January 3, 2027. Reported cash was $100,000, other current assets were $150,000, and current liabilities were $130,000. Ignoring other effects, what is the correct current ratio at December 31, 2026, rounded to two decimals?
items.rule_line: Checks not delivered by the balance sheet date remain in cash and accounts payable until mailed or otherwise delivered.

why.A: Restores the payable but not the cash. Undelivered checks remain company cash.
why.B: Correct. Checks not delivered by year-end are still company cash and the payable is still owed: (100,000 + 6,000 + 150,000) / (130,000 + 6,000) = 1.88.
why.C: This is the ratio as reported. It treats the undelivered checks as though they had been paid at year-end.
why.D: Adds the undelivered checks back to cash but leaves the payable reduced. Both cash and payables must be restored.

items.stem: Tamarack Design Inc. found these reconciling items when comparing its book balance to the December 31, 2026 bank statement: NSF customer check $1,200; interest credited by the bank $60; bank service charge $35; note collected by the bank $3,000; outstanding checks $5,400; deposit in transit $2,100. By what net amount must the company adjust its book cash balance?
items.rule_line: Only items the bank recorded but the company has not require adjustments to the company's books.

why.A: Correct. Book adjustments: +$3,000 note + $60 interest - $35 service charge - $1,200 NSF = +$1,825. Outstanding checks and the deposit in transit are bank-side items.
why.B: Ignores the NSF check, which must be deducted from book cash.
why.C: Includes the deposit in transit. It is already in the books and is a bank-side reconciling item.
why.D: Adds the NSF check. A returned check reduces book cash.

items.stem: At December 31, 2026, Sable Creek Corp. had these items: currency and coins $3,000; checking accounts $48,000; savings account $20,000; a certificate of deposit $15,000 purchased on November 1, 2026, that matures on January 31, 2027; postdated checks from customers $2,000; and a 12-month Treasury bill of $10,000 purchased on August 15, 2026. What amount is reported as cash and cash equivalents?
items.rule_line: Cash and cash equivalents include currency, demand deposits and investments with original maturities of three months or less.

why.A: Excludes the certificate of deposit. It had an original maturity of three months, so it is a cash equivalent.
why.B: Correct. Currency, checking, savings and the CD (original maturity of three months) total $86,000. Postdated checks are receivables and the 12-month bill is an investment.
why.C: Includes postdated customer checks. They cannot be deposited until their dates and are receivables.
why.D: Includes the 12-month Treasury bill. Its original maturity is far beyond three months, even though it is now within 6 months of maturity.

steps: Postdated checks are receivables; the 12-month bill is a short-term investment

items.task: Measure receivables, the allowance for credit losses, and transfers of receivables
items.task_source: 2026 AICPA Blueprint FAR Area II (group names verified; task wording paraphrased)
items.stem: An entity applies the current expected credit loss (CECL) model to its trade receivables. Which statement best describes how the allowance for credit losses is measured?
options: It records losses only when it is probable that a specific receivable has already been impaired
It measures the allowance only for receivables that are more than 90 days past due
It equals a fixed percentage of credit sales set by the industry and is not revised
It estimates lifetime expected credit losses using historical experience adjusted for current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts
items.rule_line: CECL requires lifetime expected credit losses, updated for current conditions and reasonable and supportable forecasts.

why.A: This is the former incurred-loss approach. CECL does not require a loss to be probable before it is recognized.
why.B: There is no past-due-only requirement. Expected losses are also recognized on receivables that are not yet past due.
why.C: The estimate must be updated for changes in conditions and forecasts, not held at a fixed industry percentage.
why.D: Correct. CECL reflects expected losses over the contractual life, using historical loss information adjusted for current conditions and forecasts.

items.stem: Foxglove Distributors Inc. estimates its allowance for credit losses at December 31, 2026 using the aging schedule below. Before adjustment, the allowance account has a credit balance of $7,000. What is bad debt expense for 2026?
items.rule_line: Bad debt expense equals the required allowance less the existing credit balance, or plus an existing debit balance.

why.A: Omits the over-90-days bucket ($14,000), which carries the highest loss rate.
why.B: Correct. Required allowance is $4,000 + $6,000 + $6,000 + $14,000 = $30,000. The account already holds a $7,000 credit, so expense is $23,000.
why.C: Uses the required ending balance as the expense. The existing $7,000 credit must be subtracted.
why.D: Adds the existing credit balance instead of subtracting it.

items.task: Measure receivables, the allowance for credit losses, and transfers of receivables
items.task_source: 2026 AICPA Blueprint FAR Area II (group names verified; task wording paraphrased)
items.stem: Bayview Textiles Inc. reports gross trade receivables of $250,000 and an allowance for credit losses of $18,000 (credit) at the start of a month. During the month it wrote off a $6,000 customer account, and it later collected $1,500 in cash from a different customer whose account had been written off in an earlier year. What is the net realizable value of trade receivables at the end of the month?
items.rule_line: Write-offs reduce receivables and the allowance equally; a recovery reinstates the account, crediting the allowance and then cash.

why.A: Deducts the write-off from net receivables. A write-off lowers gross receivables and the allowance equally, so net realizable value does not change.
why.B: Correct. After the write-off: receivables $244,000, allowance $12,000. The recovery reinstates the account and adds $1,500 to the allowance ($13,500), then cash is collected. Net = $244,000 - $13,500 = $230,500.
why.C: Reflects the write-off but not the recovery. Recovering a written-off account increases the allowance by $1,500, reducing the net amount.
why.D: Adds the recovery to net receivables. The cash collected reduces neither receivables nor the allowance beyond the reinstated $1,500 credit to the allowance.

steps: Recovery: Dr Receivable 1,500, Cr Allowance 1,500; Dr Cash 1,500, Cr Receivable 1,500 -> allowance 13,500, receivables 244,000

During 2026 it wrote off $14,000 of receivables and recovered $2,000 of receivables written off in prior years. At December 31, 2026, the required allowance is $25,000. What is 2026 credit loss expense?
items.rule_line: Expense equals the required ending allowance less the balance after write-offs and recoveries.

why.A: Ignores write-offs and recoveries. Both change the allowance before the year-end adjustment.
why.C: Omits the recovery. Recoveries are credited to the allowance and reduce the expense needed.
why.D: Subtracts the recovery instead of adding it to the allowance.

items.rule_line: Trade discounts reduce list price to the invoice amount; the cash discount then applies to the net invoice.

why.A: Adds the two percentages and applies them to list price. The cash discount is computed on the invoice price after the trade discount.
why.B: Correct. Trade discount first: $40,000 x 90% = $36,000. Cash discount on the net invoice: $36,000 x 98% = $35,280.
why.C: Applies only the trade discount and ignores the cash discount taken for prompt payment.
why.D: Applies only the cash discount to the list price and ignores the 10% trade discount.

items.stem: Tidewater Gear Inc. sold $500,000 of trade receivables to a factor without recourse. The transaction qualifies as a sale. The factor charged a 4% fee and withheld 5% of the receivables as a retainage that will be paid to Tidewater when customers pay. How much cash did Tidewater receive at the date of sale?
items.rule_line: In a factoring sale, cash at sale equals face amount less the fee and any retainage; retainage is a receivable.

why.A: Correct. Cash = $500,000 - $20,000 fee - $25,000 retainage = $455,000. The retainage is a receivable from the factor.
why.B: Ignores the 4% factoring fee, which is deducted from the proceeds.
why.C: Ignores the 5% retainage. It is withheld until customers pay, so it is not received at the sale date.
why.D: Assumes the factor pays the full face amount, disregarding the fee and the retainage.

items.task: Measure receivables, the allowance for credit losses, and transfers of receivables
items.task_source: 2026 AICPA Blueprint FAR Area II (group names verified; task wording paraphrased)
items.stem: Delphi Supplies Inc. transfers $300,000 of trade receivables to a bank for $270,000 with full recourse for uncollectible amounts. The receivables are legally isolated from Delphi, even in bankruptcy; the bank may pledge or sell them; and Delphi has no agreement to repurchase them before maturity and no right to reacquire specific accounts. How should Delphi account for the transfer?
options: As a secured borrowing, because recourse means the transferor keeps the risk of loss
As a secured borrowing, because the proceeds were less than the face amount
As neither a sale nor a borrowing until all receivables are collected
As a sale, because control has been surrendered; the recourse obligation is recognized at fair value
items.rule_line: A transfer of receivables is a sale if isolated, the transferee can pledge or exchange them, and the transferor keeps no effective control.

why.A: Retaining credit risk through recourse does not by itself preclude a sale. The three control conditions are met here.
why.B: Selling at a discount is common and irrelevant to the control test. The difference is a loss on sale.
why.C: Accounting is determined at the transfer date based on whether control has been surrendered, not when receivables are collected.
why.D: Correct. Sale accounting depends on isolation, the transferee's right to pledge or exchange, and no effective control by the transferor. Recourse alone does not prevent sale treatment; it is recorded as a liability.

items.stem: Which arrangement would most clearly cause a transfer of trade receivables to be accounted for as a secured borrowing rather than a sale?
options: The transferee is a bank that may resell the receivables to other investors
The receivables are placed beyond the reach of the transferor's creditors, including in bankruptcy
The transferor sells the receivables at a discount and records a loss
The transferor agrees to repurchase the receivables at a fixed price before maturity
items.rule_line: A repurchase commitment that gives the transferor effective control over transferred receivables requires borrowing treatment.

why.A: The transferee's freedom to pledge or exchange the assets supports sale treatment.
why.B: Legal isolation of the assets is one of the conditions for a sale.
why.C: A discount only affects the amount of gain or loss on the sale.
why.D: Correct. A repurchase agreement before maturity that lets the transferor keep effective control precludes sale accounting.

items.stem: On March 1, 2026, Orchard Lane Co. accepted a six-month, 6% note of $100,000 from a customer. On June 1, 2026, Orchard Lane discounted the note at a bank that charged an 8% discount rate, and the transfer qualified as a sale. What proceeds did Orchard Lane receive?
items.rule_line: Discount proceeds equal maturity value less maturity value times the discount rate for the remaining term.

why.A: Applies the discount to the face amount instead of the maturity value. The bank discounts the full amount due at maturity.
why.B: Uses six months for the discount period. Only the three months remaining after June 1 are discounted.
why.C: Correct. Maturity value = $100,000 + $3,000 interest = $103,000. Discount = $103,000 x 8% x 3/12 = $2,060. Proceeds = $100,940.
why.D: Ignores the bank's discount. Proceeds are the maturity value less the discount.

items.stem: On January 1, 2026, Granite Peak Co. sold equipment and accepted a noninterest-bearing $100,000 note due in two years. The market rate for a similar note is 10%. The equipment has no established market price. How much interest income should Granite Peak report for 2026 (rounded to the nearest dollar)?
items.rule_line: A noninterest-bearing note is recorded at present value; interest income equals carrying amount times the market rate.

why.A: Correct. Present value = $100,000 / 1.10^2 = $82,645; 2026 interest = $82,645 x 10% = $8,264 under the effective interest method.
why.B: Uses straight-line allocation of the total discount ($17,355 / 2). Interest must use the effective interest method.

items.stem: For annual periods beginning after December 15, 2025, an entity may elect a practical expedient when estimating expected credit losses on current trade receivables. What does the expedient allow?
options: It may skip recording an allowance for any receivable due within one year
It may measure the allowance only when a customer files for bankruptcy
It may record losses only when cash collection is delayed beyond 90 days
It may assume that conditions at the balance sheet date persist for the remaining life of the current receivables
items.rule_line: The optional expedient lets entities hold balance sheet conditions constant when estimating credit losses on current receivables.

why.A: The expedient simplifies how forecasts are used; it does not eliminate the allowance.
why.B: That is an incurred-loss approach and is not what the expedient permits.
why.C: Nothing in the expedient makes past-due status a trigger for recognizing expected losses.
why.D: Correct. The expedient lets an entity assume balance sheet conditions continue rather than forecasting them over the life of current accounts receivable and current contract assets.

options: Combined with trade receivables because both are receivables
As a reduction of stockholders' equity in every case
As an expense because the advance is not from a customer
Separately from trade receivables, as a receivable from an officer
items.rule_line: Receivables from officers, employees or affiliates are reported separately from trade receivables.

items.stem: Corvina Industries Inc. borrows $200,000 from a bank and assigns specific customer accounts receivable as collateral. Customers are not notified and Corvina continues to collect the accounts. Which statement about Corvina's financial statements is correct?
options: Corvina derecognizes the receivables and records a gain on sale
Corvina offsets the loan against the receivables and reports only the net
Corvina reports the receivables at fair value with changes in net income
Corvina keeps the receivables as assets, records a liability for the loan, and discloses the assigned amounts
items.rule_line: Receivables assigned as collateral for a loan stay on the balance sheet; the loan is a liability and the pledge is disclosed.

why.A: Assignment is a borrowing. No gain arises because control of the receivables is not surrendered.
why.B: Offsetting is not permitted because there is no right of setoff and no intent to settle net.
why.C: Trade receivables are not remeasured to fair value merely because they are pledged.

items.stem: Cypress Lane Inc. owes a bank $450,000 of principal plus $50,000 of accrued interest. Because of financial difficulty, the bank agreed to accept a single payment of $420,000 at maturity, with no further interest, in full settlement. What gain should Cypress Lane recognize?
items.rule_line: A debtor recognizes a gain when total future payments under the restructured terms are less than the debt's carrying amount.

why.A: Assumes no gain because payment is deferred. Total future payments are below the carrying amount.
why.B: Ignores the accrued interest of $50,000, which is part of the carrying amount.
why.C: Reports only the accrued interest as the gain.
why.D: Correct. In a restructuring with modified terms, if the total future cash payments are less than the carrying amount ($500,000), the difference of $80,000 is a gain.

items.task_source: 2026 AICPA Blueprint FAR Area II (group names verified; task wording paraphrased)
items.stem: Glacier Point Inc. owes a bank $500,000, including accrued interest. Because of financial difficulty, the bank modifies the loan: Glacier Point will repay $480,000 of principal in three years and pay interest of 4% per year ($19,200 annually) on that principal. The total future cash payments exceed the carrying amount. How should Glacier Point account for the modification?
options: A gain of $20,000 is recognized because principal was reduced from $500,000 to $480,000
A loss of $37,600 is recognized for the additional interest to be paid
No gain is recognized; the carrying amount is unchanged and a new effective rate equates the carrying amount to future payments
The old loan is extinguished and a new liability is recorded at fair value, with a gain or loss
items.rule_line: If total restructured payments exceed carrying amount, no gain is recorded and interest uses a new effective rate.

why.A: A gain arises only if total future cash payments, including interest, are below the carrying amount.
why.B: No loss is recognized; the extra payments are recognized as interest over the remaining term.
why.C: Correct. Total future payments ($480,000 + 3 x $19,200 = $537,600) exceed the carrying amount ($500,000), so no gain; interest expense is computed at the rate that equates the two.
why.D: Extinguishment accounting (new debt at fair value, gain or loss) belongs to ASC 470-50 modifications. This is a troubled debt restructuring under ASC 470-60: because total future payments exceed the carrying amount, no gain is recorded and the carrying amount is kept.

steps: Carrying amount 500,000 < 537,600 so no gain; interest 37,600 recognized over the term at a new effective rate

items.task_source: 2026 AICPA Blueprint FAR Area II (group names verified; task wording paraphrased)
items.stem: Halcyon Bay Inc. has a term loan with a carrying amount of $1,000,000. The lender and Halcyon Bay agree to new terms. The present value of the cash flows under the new terms, discounted at the original effective rate, differs by 12% from the present value under the original terms, so the modification is substantially different. The new debt has a fair value of $1,080,000, and no fees are paid. What amount is recognized as a loss on extinguishment?
items.rule_line: If the present value of cash flows changes by 10% or more, the modification is an extinguishment: new debt at fair value, difference to earnings.

why.A: Correct. A change of 10% or more is a substantial modification, treated as an extinguishment. The new debt is recorded at fair value ($1,080,000) and the loss is $80,000.
why.B: Applies the 10% substantial-modification threshold to the carrying amount as if it were the loss. The threshold only decides whether extinguishment accounting applies.
why.C: Applies the 12% present value change to carrying amount. The loss is the difference between the new debt's fair value and the old carrying amount.
why.D: Reports the fair value of the new debt as the loss.

steps: Loss = fair value of new debt 1,080,000 - carrying amount 1,000,000 = 80,000

items.rule_line: The portion of long-term debt due within one year (or operating cycle) is classified as current.

why.A: Correct. The second installment due on December 31, 2027 is $200,000, which is current at the 2026 balance sheet date.
why.B: Divides the original principal by four remaining installments; the five installments are level at $200,000 each.
why.C: This is the total remaining principal after the first payment, not just the amount due within 12 months.

items.stem: Silver Fen Corp. redeemed $5,000,000 par value bonds at 98. At the redemption date the unamortized discount was $100,000 and the unamortized debt issuance costs were $50,000. What is the result of the extinguishment?
options: A loss of $50,000
A gain of $100,000
No gain or loss
A gain of $50,000
items.rule_line: Net carrying amount of debt is par less unamortized discount and issuance costs; compare it with the reacquisition price.

why.A: Correct. Reacquisition price = $4,900,000; net carrying amount = $5,000,000 - $100,000 - $50,000 = $4,850,000. Price exceeds carrying amount by $50,000, a loss.
why.B: Compares the price with par ($5,000,000 - $4,900,000) and ignores the discount and issuance costs.
why.C: Uses net carrying amount excluding issuance costs ($4,900,000), which equals the price. Unamortized issuance costs also reduce the carrying amount.
why.D: Reverses the direction. The price paid is above the net carrying amount, so there is a loss.

items.stem: Which statement about amortizing a bond discount or premium is correct?
options: Straight-line amortization is required for bonds issued at a premium
Premiums are amortized but discounts are not amortized
Amortization is not required if the bonds are held to maturity
The effective interest method is required unless straight-line amortization produces a result that is not materially different
items.rule_line: Use the effective interest method to amortize discounts and premiums; straight-line is allowed only if not materially different.

why.A: There is no such rule. The effective interest method is the primary approach.
why.B: Both discounts and premiums are amortized over the life of the debt.
why.C: The issuer must amortize regardless of the holder's intent.
why.D: Correct. Interest should be recognized using the effective interest method; straight-line is acceptable if the difference from the effective method is immaterial.

items.stem: On January 1, 2026, Quarry Bend Inc. issued $1,000,000 par value, 6% bonds due in five years with annual interest paid December 31. The bonds were issued to yield 8% and the issue price was $920,146. What is interest expense for 2027 (nearest dollar)?
items.rule_line: Each year's effective interest expense equals the beginning carrying amount times the market rate.

why.A: This is cash interest at the stated rate.
why.B: Repeats 2026's expense. The carrying amount grew, so 2027 interest is higher.
why.C: Correct. 2026 expense = $920,146 x 8% = $73,612; discount amortization = $13,612; carrying amount at 12/31/2026 = $933,758; 2027 expense = $933,758 x 8% = $74,701.
why.D: Applies the market rate to par instead of to the carrying amount.

items.stem: Vale Crest Inc. issues preferred shares that must be redeemed for cash on a fixed date in five years. How should the shares be classified?
options: As equity, because they are legally shares
As mezzanine equity between liabilities and stockholders' equity
As a liability, because the shares embody an unconditional obligation to transfer cash
As a contra asset offsetting investments
items.rule_line: Shares that must be redeemed for cash on a fixed or determinable date are liabilities, not equity.

why.A: Legal form does not determine classification; the obligation to redeem makes them liabilities.
why.B: Mezzanine presentation is used for redeemable shares that are not mandatorily redeemable (SEC registrants) and does not apply here.
why.C: Correct. Mandatorily redeemable financial instruments are classified as liabilities.
why.D: Such shares are financing instruments and are not offset against assets.

items.rule_line: Zero-coupon debt accrues interest expense at the effective rate on its carrying amount, increasing the liability.

why.A: Assumes no interest expense because no cash interest is paid. Interest accrues through discount amortization.
why.B: Correct. Interest expense = $712,986 x 7% = $49,909, added to the carrying amount because no cash interest is paid.
why.C: Uses straight-line amortization of the discount. Effective interest is required.
why.D: Applies 7% to the face amount instead of the carrying amount.

items.stem: Willow Gate Inc. issued 10-year bonds at a premium and uses the effective interest method. Which pattern describes the years after issuance?
options: Interest expense increases each year and the carrying amount decreases toward face value
Interest expense stays constant and the carrying amount decreases toward face value
Interest expense decreases each year and the carrying amount decreases toward face value
Interest expense decreases each year and the carrying amount increases above face value
items.rule_line: For a premium bond, effective interest expense falls as the carrying amount amortizes down toward face value.

why.A: Expense is based on carrying amount, which is falling, so expense falls too.
why.B: Only cash interest is constant. Expense declines as the carrying amount declines.
why.C: Correct. As the premium amortizes, the carrying amount falls, so interest expense (carrying amount x market rate) declines while cash interest stays constant.
why.D: A premium is amortized down toward face value; the carrying amount does not rise.

options: The entire amount is credited to common stock
$1,000 to common stock and $49,000 to additional paid-in capital
The entire amount is credited to additional paid-in capital
The entire amount is credited to retained earnings
items.rule_line: For no-par stock with no stated value, the entire proceeds are credited to common stock.

why.A: Correct. With no par or stated value, all proceeds are credited to common stock.
why.B: There is no par value to allocate. Nothing is credited to APIC.
why.C: Proceeds from no-par stock are credited to common stock.

items.rule_line: Assets acquired for stock are recorded at the fair value of the assets or of the stock, whichever is more clearly determinable.

why.B: Records the land at par value of the shares issued.
why.C: Records the excess over par only.

items.task_source: 2026 AICPA Blueprint FAR Area II (group names verified; task wording paraphrased)
items.stem: Elmwood Bay Inc. uses the cost method for treasury stock. It repurchased 5,000 shares at $30. It later resold 2,000 shares at $36 and then 1,000 shares at $26. Additional paid-in capital from treasury stock had no balance before these sales. What is the balance in additional paid-in capital from treasury stock after both sales?
items.rule_line: Resale above cost credits APIC-treasury; resale below cost debits APIC-treasury first, then retained earnings.

why.A: Reports only the loss on the second sale.
why.B: Correct. The first sale credits APIC-treasury for $6 x 2,000 = $12,000. The second sale at $4 below cost first reduces APIC-treasury by $4,000, leaving $8,000.
why.C: Ignores the second sale below cost, which reduces APIC from treasury stock.
why.D: Uses the difference between the two resale prices without regard to cost.

steps: First sale: 2,000 x (36 - 30) = 12,000 credit to APIC-treasury
Second sale: 1,000 x (30 - 26) = 4,000 debit to APIC-treasury

items.stem: Hollis Fen Inc. originally issued common stock for $50 per share ($10 par) and later repurchased and retired 1,000 shares at $42 per share. Which treatment is acceptable when the shares are retired?
options: Recognize an $8,000 gain in net income
Recognize an $8,000 gain in other comprehensive income
Credit retained earnings for $42,000 as a return of capital
Remove the shares' par value and original paid-in capital, and credit the $8,000 excess of the original issue price over the repurchase price to additional paid-in capital
items.rule_line: Retiring shares never creates income; a price below original issue is credited to APIC, above issue is charged to APIC then retained earnings.

why.A: Transactions in a company's own shares never produce gains or losses in income.
why.B: OCI is not affected by transactions in the entity's own equity.
why.C: The repurchase price is not credited to retained earnings.
why.D: Correct. When the repurchase price is below the original issue price, the difference may be credited to additional paid-in capital (retirement) rather than income.

items.stem: Riverside Terrace Corp. has 100,000 shares of $5 par common stock outstanding. It declares and distributes a 10% stock dividend when the market price is $20 per share. By what amount is retained earnings reduced?
items.rule_line: A small stock dividend is recorded at fair value, reducing retained earnings and increasing common stock and APIC.

why.A: Assumes no reduction because no cash is distributed. A stock dividend transfers retained earnings to contributed capital.
why.B: Uses par value, which applies to large stock dividends.
why.C: Correct. A small stock dividend (below 20-25%) is recorded at fair value: 10,000 shares x $20 = $200,000, capitalized from retained earnings.

Total stockholders' equity doubles because more shares exist
items.rule_line: A stock split changes the number of shares and per-share par but not total equity or its components.

why.B: With unchanged par, the total par amount would double, which changes the capital accounts.

items.stem: Redbank Corp.'s retained earnings were $900,000 at January 1, 2026. During 2026 it earned net income of $250,000, declared and paid cash dividends of $90,000, and distributed a small stock dividend recorded at $60,000. It also sold treasury shares for $15,000 less than cost, and there was no additional paid-in capital from treasury stock available. What is retained earnings at December 31, 2026?
items.rule_line: Retained earnings falls for cash and stock dividends and for treasury losses in excess of APIC-treasury.

why.A: Correct. $900,000 + $250,000 - $90,000 cash dividends - $60,000 stock dividend - $15,000 treasury loss charged to retained earnings = $985,000.
why.B: Omits the treasury stock loss charged to retained earnings when APIC-treasury is exhausted.
why.C: Omits the stock dividend, which transfers retained earnings to contributed capital.
why.D: Omits the cash dividends.

steps: Less cash dividends 90,000, stock dividend 60,000, treasury loss 15,000
